claims: Jump identity must distinguish the starting action, projection direction, takeoff and landing laterality, external height or obstacle, rebound intent, and required stabilization.
{{canonicalName}} must not combine a paused static start, countermovement, repeated rebound, loaded jump, testing protocol, or different landing laterality under one unspecified card.
A jump-to-stick combines ballistic propulsion with a deliberate landing and stabilization phase; repeated reactive hopping is a different programming task.
{{canonicalName}} belongs to jump power with landing control, with direction, laterality, initiation, flight action, and rebound intent encoded as controlled dimensions.
Propulsion and force absorption are coordinated across the foot and ankle, knee, hip, pelvis, and trunk.

The card should assign task-specific roles to plantar flexors and intrinsic foot muscles, quadriceps, hamstrings, gluteals, hip stabilizers, and trunk stabilizers rather than naming one isolated muscle.
Jump demand changes with projection speed, direction, external height, body mass, and the time available to produce and absorb force.

Observable quality includes the prescribed initiation, coordinated ankle-knee-hip propulsion, intended flight path, re-extension before contact where needed, quiet whole-foot landing, knee tracking, trunk control, and ownership of the finish.
Plyometric intensity changes with speed, height, distance, body mass, external load, laterality, and movement complexity.

Exercise difficulty must score technical complexity and physical demand directly, including coordination, impact, supervision, work capacity, and consequence of error; an exercise card must not receive a skill-library level.
Landing contacts, jump height or distance, approach and initiation, laterality, and external load govern mechanical exposure; high-quality power repetitions require adequate rest.

{{canonicalName}} needs contact count, intent, impact and eccentric stress, technical-fatigue sensitivity, performance-loss criteria, and recovery guidance instead of treating all jumps as conditioning repetitions.
Effective jump-landing interventions depend on appropriate materials, coaching knowledge, usable space, and task-specific progression.

The delivery profile should require a level non-slip surface, clear flight and landing zones, adequate ceiling height, suitable footwear, athlete spacing, coach sightline, and readiness for the prescribed landing demand.
Landing and stabilization control should precede higher, farther, unilateral, repeated, or reactive jumping.
Prescribe low-repetition quality sets, contacts, intent, target height or distance where relevant, hold duration, rest, and progression criteria; stop before fatigue alters takeoff or landing.
Specific prescriptive feedback can improve jump-landing mechanics, while excessive cue volume can interfere with learning.
Use a small cue set tied to the identity: perform the prescribed start, project in the intended direction, land quietly, align foot-knee-hip, and hold without a touch-down, shuffle, or rebound.
Loud contact, poor stabilization, loss of alignment, or inability to coordinate ankle, knee, and hip indicate that jump intensity or volume exceeds current control.
Stop for pain, giving way, dizziness, repeated valgus or trunk collapse, uncontrolled foot contact, failure to re-extend before landing, missed landing zone, extra steps, or loss of jump output.
Landing stabilization and lower-body strength are recurring components of effective neuromuscular injury-prevention programs.
{{canonicalName}} belongs after preparation and before fatigued conditioning; high-intent jump work should use low volume and full enough recovery to preserve output and landing quality.
Athletes benefit from feedback tied to visible movement actions rather than abstract risk language.
Athlete support should show the start, flight, and landing shapes, define a successful repetition, identify the target and hold time, provide one primary cue, and explain the stop signal.
Coach education and practical implementation affect whether jump-landing interventions are delivered effectively.

Coach support should provide front and side observation points, pass-fail criteria, contact counting, output-loss and asymmetry rules, progressions, regressions, equipment checks, and rules for reducing height, distance, laterality, or cue complexity.
Beginners should establish bilateral landing and stabilization before progressing to unilateral, higher, farther, or reactive tasks.

Accessibility can be improved with visual targets, demonstrated shapes, plain-language cues, reduced height or distance, assistance, longer reset time, and reduced sensory or decision load without assigning an exercise skill level.
Static starts, countermovements, jumps covering distance, unilateral landings, repeated contacts, obstacles, and externally loaded jumps have different intensity and programming implications.

Arm action, target distance, submaximal intent, and assistance are usually variants or modifiers; different initiation, projection, landing laterality, rebound intent, or testing purpose may require a distinct definition.
YouTube supports privacy-enhanced embedding through youtube-nocookie.com.

The direct candidates for {{canonicalName}} were discovered or rechecked through visible YouTube search and public oEmbed metadata; exact movement match, full-content review, captions, instructional quality, safety, and approval remain pending human review.

assessmentSummary.identity: A bilateral vertical jump initiated from a motionless partial-squat hold, followed by a bilateral landing in the takeoff area and a deliberate two-second stick.
currentCardFindings: The legacy card does not specify a pause, so it overlaps the separate Countermovement Jump to Stick identity.
Its generic 40-point scoring understates impact and failure consequence while leaving supervision, impact, and work-capacity demand unscored.
Anatomy, controlled taxonomy, load, fatigue, constraints, and support fields are empty; one repetition at RPE 9 does not define start depth, pause, jump intent, landing hold, or progression.

proposedDosage.progressWhen: the athlete holds the same squat depth, jumps without a countermovement, and lands quietly in the takeoff area on every repetition

coachCues: Set the squat depth and become still
Jump straight up without dipping again
athleteInstructions: Hold a shallow squat for two seconds
Jump straight up from the still position
Land on both feet and hold

readiness: mastered snap-down and basic bilateral jump landing

assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Rename to Paused Squat Jump to Stick or require a two-to-three-second static start in every profile. The separate countermovement card owns a rapid dip-and-drive; do not treat the two starts as interchangeable.

alternateAssessments.name: Paused Squat Jump to Stick
alternateAssessments.rationale: The pause makes the intended static-start identity explicit and separates it from a countermovement jump.

alternateAssessments.name: Countermovement Jump to Stick
alternateAssessments.rationale: A rapid eccentric dip before takeoff changes initiation, stretch-shortening contribution, and timing demand.

alternateAssessments.name: Arm-Restricted Paused Squat Jump
alternateAssessments.rationale: Hands-on-hips execution changes arm contribution but preserves the static bilateral vertical jump.

alternateAssessments.name: Band-Assisted Squat Jump to Stick
alternateAssessments.rationale: Assistance reduces effective load and landing demand while preserving the start and projection.

alternateAssessments.name: Repeated Jump Squats
alternateAssessments.rationale: Continuous rebounds remove the stick and emphasize reactive output or work capacity.

assessmentSummary.identity: A bilateral vertical jump using one rapid self-selected countermovement and arm swing, followed by a bilateral landing in place and a deliberate two-second stick.
currentCardFindings: The legacy description identifies dip-and-drive but does not lock out repeated bouncing, loaded execution, testing protocols, or landing laterality.
Its generic 40-point difficulty does not score impact, supervision, failure consequence, or output-related fatigue.
Controlled taxonomy, anatomy, load, fatigue, constraints, and coach/athlete support are empty.

proposedDosage.progressWhen: one clean dip produces vertical projection and all landings remain quiet, symmetrical, and in place without output loss

coachCues: Drive the floor away and finish tall
athleteInstructions: Dip once and jump straight up
Land on both feet and hold for two seconds

readiness: mastered bilateral landing and paused jump to stick

assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Retain as the single-repetition dip-and-drive jump-to-stick. Keep paused squat jumps, loaded jumps, repeated countermovement jumps, and formal jump testing as variants or separate contextual profiles.

assessmentSummary.identity: A standing bilateral countermovement jump projected forward for distance, followed by a bilateral landing and deliberate stabilization without an extra step.
currentCardFindings: The legacy description incorrectly frames this as jump-height work even though the defining vector is horizontal distance.
The one-repetition RPE 9 profile does not distinguish training from a standardized standing broad-jump test or prescribe distance, landing zone, hold, and output-loss rules.
Generic 40-point difficulty and empty anatomy, load, fatigue, constraints, and support fields understate horizontal momentum and landing consequence.

proposedDosage.progressWhen: projection is symmetrical and repeated distance stays stable while every landing remains quiet and held behind the safety boundary

coachCues: Load the hips and swing the arms
Reach the feet forward then bring the hips over them
athleteInstructions: Land on two feet and hold without stepping
commonFaults: feet too far ahead of hips

assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Retain as horizontal projection and braking, not jump-height work. Separate the standardized standing broad-jump assessment profile from submaximal learning and high-intent training profiles.

assessmentSummary.identity: A vertical jump from a split stance with the same lead leg retained through flight and a controlled landing back into the same split stance; the current card is quarantined because it also permits switching legs.
currentCardFindings: The cue 'switch or land split' combines same-stance split-squat jumps and scissor jumps, which have different coordination and landing demands.
The generic 40-point score does not represent split-stance balance, front-leg braking, pelvis control, impact, or consequence of error.
Anatomy, load, fatigue, constraints, laterality, and support fields are empty; the current media pool must be reviewed for same-side versus switching execution.

proposedDosage.progressWhen: the same lead leg is retained and both sides land on their marks with stable foot, knee, pelvis, and trunk

coachCues: Land back on the same marks
Own the front foot, knee, and pelvis
athleteInstructions: Jump straight up and keep the same leg forward
Land in the same stance and hold

readiness: stable split-stance landing on both lead sides

assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Quarantine until the contact sequence is fixed. Preferred base identity retains the same lead leg; create a Scissor Jump to Stick variant or definition for an intentional mid-air switch and do not permit both under one instruction.

assessmentSummary.identity: A single high-intent bilateral vertical jump with a deliberate knee-tuck action during flight, active leg re-extension before contact, and a bilateral landing held for two seconds.
currentCardFindings: The legacy description identifies knee drive and re-extension but prescribes three repetitions and 20 work seconds, which risks turning a high-impact skill into a repeated fatigue drill.
The generic 40-point difficulty substantially understates flight coordination, re-extension timing, impact, supervision, and consequence of error.
Controlled anatomy, load, fatigue, constraints, and support fields are empty; repeated tuck jumps and obstacle or block variations are not separated.

proposedDosage.progressWhen: the knees rise without trunk collapse, legs fully re-extend before contact, and every landing remains quiet and held

coachCues: Bring knees up without folding the chest
Straighten the legs before the floor
athleteInstructions: Tuck your knees in the air
Land on both feet and hold

readiness: mastered high-intent countermovement jump to stick

assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Retain only as a single-repetition reset drill with active re-extension and full landing ownership. Continuous tuck jumps, work intervals, and block-drop tuck jumps require separate definitions or profiles and higher exposure controls.

alternateAssessments.name: Single Tuck Jump and Stick
alternateAssessments.rationale: This name makes the required single repetition, reset, and landing stabilization explicit.

alternateAssessments.name: Submaximal Tuck Jump to Target
alternateAssessments.rationale: A lower knee target reduces flight demand while preserving the tuck and re-extension sequence.

alternateAssessments.name: Continuous Tuck Jumps
alternateAssessments.rationale: Repeated rebound contacts remove the stick and sharply increase reactive and metabolic exposure.

alternateAssessments.name: Tuck Jump Off Block to Stick
alternateAssessments.rationale: External drop height increases flight and landing demand and requires stable equipment and separate dosage.

alternateAssessments.name: Countermovement Jump to Stick
alternateAssessments.rationale: Removing the in-flight tuck is the direct lower-coordination regression while retaining vertical projection and landing.
